Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Several features outside of the conventional assumptions in traditional item response theory (IRT) models have been revealed to be related, yet no unifying framework explains the features simultaneously.
They can be unified by treating each cause as a distinct reason, and then regarding every reason as a choice in a latent multiple-choice item.
Here, we propose the Microstate Response Model (MiRM), which decomposes each response category (macrostate) into multiple latent reasons (microstates) using Boltzmann weights.

The consequences of this simple framework are substantial; for example, it reads the lower and upper asymptotes of item characteristic curves (ICCs) as additional states, and ICC asymmetry and item complexity as multiple states.
The model unifies many classical models from the dichotomous logistic family to mixture models.
Moreover, the algebra of the model provides the intuition that items and tests are the same object.
Two consequences naturally come out: partial credits and test scores are unified, and a new test-level monotonicity condition is proposed.

We examine item characteristics including nonmonotonicity on PISA 2015, and show that MiRM provides a deeper understanding of items while achieving the strongest overall performance across fit, parsimony, and prediction.
Item response theory (IRT) aims to estimate a person's latent trait or ability from item response data, and further understand each item's characteristics that enable the measurement.

Since the true latent ability cannot be observed, the theory typically assumes certain properties of the items (Rasch, 1960) and the trait (Holland & Rosenbaum, 1986; Sijtsma, 1998), thereby making persons and items identifiable and interpretable on a common scale.
text.formatted: Since the true latent ability cannot be observed, the theory typically assumes certain properties of the items <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Rasch, 1960)</ref> and the trait <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Holland & Rosenbaum, 1986;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Sijtsma, 1998)</ref>, thereby making persons and items identifiable and interpretable on a common scale.

text.text: For example, the characteristics of an item should not depend on which group of respondents takes it, the same ability should be obtained regardless of which items are used, no variable other than the ability should explain the responses, and a higher ability should lead to a higher probability of a correct response.
In fact, not every assumption holds perfectly in real-world data.
For example, respondents sometimes answer correctly by chance or wrongly by mistake, and items may work differently for different groups of respondents.

We call these exceptions departures from the conventional IRT assumptions, and many of them appear in the shapes of item characteristic curves (ICCs), which show how the probability of a correct response changes with ability.
One approach to resolving the tension between theory and practice is to model the mechanism that is believed to generate each departure, by adding a parameter for it.

The 3-parameter logistic (3PL) model adds a guessing parameter 𝑝 𝑐 , as low-ability respondents sometimes 'guess' the answer, thereby keeping the lower asymptote of its ICC -the probability of a correct response at the lowest abilitiesabove zero (Birnbaum, 1968).

text.text: The 4-parameter logistic (4PL) model (Barton & Lord, 1981) likewise adds a parameter for high-ability respondents who 'slip' through careless mistakes, thereby keeping the upper asymptote below one.

text.text: Furthermore, some empirical ICCs are asymmetric; they rise steeply on one side and slowly on the other.

The Logistic Positive Exponent (LPE; Samejima, 2000) model and the Residual Heteroscedasticity (RH; Molenaar, 2015) model tried to capture this asymmetry by adding interpretable parameters: an exponent parameter in the LPE model, and a population-level heteroscedasticity parameter in the RH model, which lets the randomness of the responses differ across ability levels.

text.text: As can be seen, each departure has usually been studied individually, and the shapes of ICCs are categorized differently across fields.

However, several recent studies have revealed that such departures are closely related to each other, and also to the complexity of an item, such as the number of steps needed to solve it (Bolt & Liao, 2022; Bolt et al., 2018; Lee & Bolt, 2018b; Liao & Bolt, 2021).

text.text: In addition, Culpepper (2016) and Meng et al. (2020) showed that the 4PL model can be understood as a mixture model with careless and guessing groups.

text.text: These relationships also mean that a parameter does not always describe what its name suggests; the guessing parameter, for example, may in fact be describing asymmetry, and what we learn about an item then depends on which model we choose.

Although these relationships have been formalized through systematic definitions (Feuerstahler et al., 2026; Shim & Bonifay, 2026), a unified model conceptually combining the departures remains absent.

text.text: If we take a step back, the various mechanisms above can be reduced to a single cause.
A correct answer from a lucky guess is recorded simply as correct, and a wrong answer from a careless mistake simply as wrong.
A difficult and complex item makes people fail for different reasons, while an item open to many shortcuts lets people succeed for different reasons.
Seen within a single item, the fact that people respond differently according to their ability levels or dispositions also means that the same response can be chosen for different reasons.
Therefore, every response suffers an information loss, as it does not record the 'reason' for the choice.
Item formats that record such reasons already exist.
Interviews and essay questions are typical examples, and polytomous items, which record which option was chosen rather than only whether it was correct, are a more standardized form.
Many models have brought such detailed information into IRT; let us consider the most basic one, the Nominal Response Model (NRM; Bock, 1972).
text.formatted: Many models have brought such detailed information into IRT; let us consider the most basic one, the Nominal Response Model (NRM; <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Bock, 1972)</ref>.

text.text: Noting that not all distractors, the wrong options of an item, are chosen in the same pattern, Bock gave each distractor its own exponential term so that they could be analyzed individually.
Applying this idea to any dichotomous item, one could suspect that several latent distractors lie behind its single wrong response.
If so, what prevents us from asking whether information about the correct response has likewise been lost?
Any response, correct or wrong, can have more than one reason, as the lucky guess above already shows.
Both can therefore be decomposed into latent 'reasons for the response' from the perspective of polytomous IRT, even though the reasons are not observed.

This approach is not new: Maris (1995) introduced latent responses and their condensation into an observed response as general modeling principles, and related ideas appear in the Nested Logit Model (NLM; Suh & Bolt, 2010) and in IRTree models, which describe a response as the end of a sequence of latent decisions (Böckenholt, 2012; De Boeck & Partchev, 2012).
text.formatted: This approach is not new: <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Maris (1995)</ref> introduced latent responses and their condensation into an observed response as general modeling principles, and related ideas appear in the Nested Logit Model (NLM; <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Suh & Bolt, 2010)</ref> and in IRTree models, which describe a response as the end of a sequence of latent decisions <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Böckenholt, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">De Boeck & Partchev, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Even within ratios-of-sums-ofexponentials, there have been 'don't know' models (Samejima, 1979; Thissen & Steinberg, 1984) and their subsequent extensions (Jin et al., 2022; Shigemasu & Ueno, 1993; Thissen et al., 1989) that assume a latent 'guessed response' category.
text.formatted: Even within ratios-of-sums-ofexponentials, there have been 'don't know' models <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Samejima, 1979;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Thissen & Steinberg, 1984)</ref> and their subsequent extensions <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Jin et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Shigemasu & Ueno, 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Thissen et al., 1989</ref>) that assume a latent 'guessed response' category.

text.text: However, our model differs from these models because we assume that the number of reasons and their exact cognitive counterparts are also unknown.
Hence, we allow an arbitrary number of terms, which comes at a price: each term can be identified only partially from the responses, and the number of terms has to be chosen for each item.
Yet being unable to identify a reason exactly does not mean that we should leave it unused.
We therefore make room for latent reasons, and let data decide the configuration.
Under this simple assumption, applying the NRM to the latent 'reasons' yields a model that we call the Microstate Response Model (MiRM).
text.formatted: Under this simple assumption, applying the NRM to the latent 'reasons' yields a model that we call the Microstate Response Model <ref type="bibr">(MiRM)</ref>.

text.text: The terminology comes from statistical mechanics (Landau & Lifshitz, 2013), where microstates are the distinct states of a system, some of which cannot be distinguished by macroscopic observation, and a macrostate is a coarse-grained state, that is, a group of microstates that show the same observation.
text.formatted: The terminology comes from statistical mechanics <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Landau & Lifshitz, 2013)</ref>, where microstates are the distinct states of a system, some of which cannot be distinguished by macroscopic observation, and a macrostate is a coarse-grained state, that is, a group of microstates that show the same observation.

text.text: Thus, a macrostate corresponds to an observed response as an aggregation of its latent reasons, and microstates correspond to the reasons.

This correspondence is more than an analogy, as it brings mathematical tools and interpretations. Smith and Bendjilali (2022) captured the similarity between the NRM and the canonical ensemble, the Boltzmann distribution over the states of a system, by relating the energy of each state to the discrimination of each response option.
text.formatted: This correspondence is more than an analogy, as it brings mathematical tools and interpretations. <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Smith and Bendjilali (2022)</ref> captured the similarity between the NRM and the canonical ensemble, the Boltzmann distribution over the states of a system, by relating the energy of each state to the discrimination of each response option.

text.text: They further examined whether the concept of coarse-graining can be applied.
However, they did not define IRT counterparts to 'microstates'; the absence is where our approach begins.
The microstates put the 'reasons' that have been modeled separately on a single layer.
If we regard guessing as a microstate, it keeps a share of correct responses even among the least able respondents, and MiRM reduces to the 3PL model.
More generally, MiRM reads departures such as the asymptotes, asymmetry, item complexity, and nonmonotonicity directly from its item parameters, instead of adding a new parameter for each of them.

The item discrimination 𝑎 and difficulty 𝑏 of the 2-parameter logistic (2PL; Birnbaum, 1968) model, which tell how sharply and at which ability an item distinguishes respondents, have been diluted by such additional parameters.

text.text: MiRM restores them as functions of ability, 𝑎(𝜃) and 𝑏(𝜃), that can be identified from the ICC.
Furthermore, the framework covers nonparametric IRT models through the Universal Approximation Theorem (Theorem 4.1), providing them with an interpretable algebraic lens.
This approach does not stop at combining existing item models; it naturally covers an object beyond the item level as well.

Just as an item discards the reasons behind a response and compresses them into a single observed response, psychometrics has one more response system that discards the hidden information behind several responses and compresses them into a single result: a test.
Although a test has been regarded as a set of items, it is an item itself.

Following this intuition, we prove algebraically that an item and a test are the same object under MiRM, and from this we unify partial credits and total scores, which have been regarded as different objects.
Therefore, the monotonicity condition that has been imposed on each item can be moved to the test, the unit that actually measures ability.
We can thereby model items that show nonmonotonic ICCs in real data while keeping the ability scale meaningful.
The core contributions of this paper are itemwise model unification, item-test equivalence and a new test-level condition, and validation through large-scale datasets.

Overall, by proposing MiRM, we aim to observe how the theoretical microstates represent practical structures in empirical data, without introducing departure-specific item parameters to resolve the tension between theory and practice.
In doing so, we recover part of the information lost in the responses, thereby identifying individual ability precisely and providing a better understanding of items.

Section 4 introduces how MiRM unifies existing models, and describes how the nonstandard item characteristics are read from microstates throughout the unification process.
Section 5 shows that the estimation of MiRM follows the standard protocol of existing IRT models, and illustrates how the test-level condition is satisfied in implementation.

The resulting model is assessed with respect to its fit performance, prediction, ability recovery, identification, and interpretation of item characteristics on both synthetic (Section 6) and empirical (Section 7) data.
Further implications and limitations are discussed in Section 8.

text.text: One reason for developing a single framework for items and tests is to allow individual items to have locally nonmonotonic ICCs without losing the meaning of ability.
If 𝜃 served only as a coordinate that improves model fit, it would not constitute a measurement scale.
IRT therefore requires a condition under which greater ability provides stronger evidence of successful performance.
Itemwise monotonicity offers a direct way to impose this requirement and has consequently been treated as a central assumption of unidimensional IRT.

It may be sufficient, however, rather than necessary: previous studies have suggested that respondents may remain ordered even when some individual ICCs are nonmonotonic (Feuerstahler et al., 2024; Junker, 1993; Stout, 1990).

text.text: We likewise seek to identify individual ability by imposing a monotonicity constraint at the test level, as we measure ability using tests, but usually not a single item.
However, the major challenge of defining monotonicity at the test level is that there are a lot of aggregate statistics for multiple items, but none of them are fully credible.
We do not know which items weigh more, how to average them, and even whether their importance varies over ability, before we assess the data.
Hence, we rely on two criteria: the all-correct pattern C and the all-distractor pattern D, which were used above to define the generalized credit.

When neither the ordering of items, the number of similar or duplicated items, nor any arbitrary scores or weights assigned to them are taken as trustworthy, these are the only two states that remain invariant under any monotone rescoring.

PRM is intentionally weaker than SOM, to allow us to capture individual items' local nonmonotonicity.
Although PRM may appear to weaken the overall monotonicity condition, it still gives four guarantees together with the generalized credit (Theorem A.2).
First, different abilities give different response distributions, so ability is identifiable.
Second, the ability scale keeps a single direction, even when the true trait is multidimensional.
Third, a pattern with a higher generalized credit gives stronger evidence of higher ability.
Fourth, the expected generalized score T (𝜃) = E [𝑇 (X; 𝜃) | 𝜃] stays between 0 and 𝐽.
Conversely, without PRM, models that allow nonmonotonic ICCs, including MiRM, are prone to recover a wrong ability direction.

The number of microstates can differ across items.
The model having a different microstate configuration (𝑐, 𝑑) per item is called the per-item MiRM, or MiRM(𝑐 𝑗 , 𝑑 𝑗 ).

To search for the best configuration for each item, four adjacent models MiRM(𝑐 𝑗 , 𝑑 𝑗 ), MiRM(𝑐 𝑗 , 𝑑 𝑗 + 1), MiRM(𝑐 𝑗 + 1, 𝑑 𝑗 ), and MiRM(𝑐 𝑗 + 1, 𝑑 𝑗 + 1) are trained simultaneously for every item 𝑗 ∈ {1, . . . , 𝐽}, with all four models sharing 𝑐 𝑗 correct microstates and 𝑑 𝑗 distractor microstates.

Without sharing these base microstates, fitting the four models separately always favors the largest configuration, whereas sharing them forces the base states to remain meaningful across all four models and prevents unconstrained growth of the state counts.
After the training is done, (𝑐 𝑗 , 𝑑 𝑗 ) is shifted to a preferred direction under a shared ability posterior θ, and then the training resumes.

The preferred direction is determined by four conditions: for example, to shift toward a larger 𝑑 𝑗 for each item 𝑗, (𝑐 𝑗 , 𝑑 𝑗 + 1) must improve on (𝑐 𝑗 , 𝑑 𝑗 ), (𝑐 𝑗 + 1, 𝑑 𝑗 + 1) must improve on (𝑐 𝑗 + 1, 𝑑 𝑗 ), and both improvements must still hold after subtracting their mean across all items.
The loss of each model is calculated under the geometric mean of the four models' ability posteriors.
The cycle terminates when no (𝑐 𝑗 , 𝑑 𝑗 ) is shifted after training.
To select the smallest number of microstates, we start from (𝑐 𝑗 , 𝑑 𝑗 ) = (1, 1) for every item at the first cycle.
A full illustration of the estimation procedure is provided in Appendix D.2.

Reading 22 is scored correct only when all three yes-or-no judgments are correct.
The probability of getting all three right by random guessing is 0.125, almost identical to the overall proportion correct of 0.126.
Yet the fitted ICC is near chance at low ability, falls below chance at intermediate ability, and rises again at high ability.
An overall proportion near chance does not mean that everyone guessed.
Above-chance performance at high ability and below-chance performance at intermediate ability can offset each other in the overall average; the ICC separates the two.
In every data split, the per-item MiRM selected at least two correct microstates and more than two distractor microstates for Reading 22 (Figure 5).

text.text: This is consistent with an item that can be answered correctly through knowledge or chance, but can be answered incorrectly in several ways.

The observed subitem responses show this pathway directly: while the correct pattern (Yes, No, No) accounts for 12.6%, the most common pattern is (Yes, No, Yes) at 56.4%, missing only the final judgment.

Across rest-score deciles (proportion correct on the remaining items in the domain), the first two judgments increase monotonically, whereas the final judgment drops from 33% in the first decile to 17% in the fifth before rising to 38% in the tenth.
Intermediate students who resolve the first two judgments but favor the wrong answer on the last one therefore fall below the all-three guessing rate.
Science 81, Weather Balloon, is a four-option multiple-choice item.

The correct option (Option 2) states that the balloon's material cannot be stretched any farther, whereas 79% of incorrect respondents selected the option that the pressure inside increases (Option 4).

Across rest-score deciles, the selection rates of Options 1 and 3 decrease monotonically, whereas Option 4 peaks at 68% in the sixth decile as Option 2 dips to 16% in the third decile, showing that the local decline is driven by a single competing response rather than errors dispersed across the options.
Mathematics 42 requires both of two yes-or-no judgments to be correct, giving a chance probability of 0.25.

The left portion of its fitted ICC is higher than that of Reading 22, which requires three correct judgments; here too, the observed proportion correct and the ICC both decline at intermediate ability.
In these three examples, nonmonotonicity is a decline over a limited ability range, not a reversal over the entire scale.
Its location and height can be read alongside the item's scoring and option structure.

As unidimensional IRT models place all respondents on a single scale, they seek the ability path that the test supports the most, even if the true ability space is multidimensional.
Here, PRM prevents the path from being reversed in the ability space (Theorem A.2(ii)).

The PISA dataset provides such an opportunity: since many students take forms across domains, we can regard the full-bank data combining the three domains as a single dataset and then fit the model.
Furthermore, since the full bank contains the items of each domain, the ability scale of the full bank can be compared with the abilities obtained from each domain in the previous analyses.
We therefore draw the ability scale of the full bank as a path in the three-dimensional space made of the three domain abilities, and examine how the path is drawn.
We fitted the per-item MiRM to the three PISA domains together as a single 241-item bank, once with PRM and once without PRM (Figure 9).

When different combinations of domain performance are placed on one dimension, a single path cannot branch; it can turn back to follow another direction and thereby represent some of those differences.
This representation comes with a small gain in training likelihood, but within a folded region a larger 𝜃 no longer means better overall performance.

text.text: >Discussion
text.formatted: <head n="8." >Discussion</head>

text.text: Traditional IRT models have worked well because they provide economical descriptions of corresponding psychometric item characteristics.
Parameters for guessing-like behavior, slipping-like behavior, item complexity, or residual heteroscedasticity efficiently represent lower and upper asymptotes, and ICC asymmetry.
However, item characteristics vary even among items within the same testlet, and introducing a separate parameterization for each departure does not explain why these characteristics are related.
MiRM offers a different level of explanation through a single principle: an observed response is a coarse-grained outcome of competition among latent response states.
From this perspective, the results of this paper are not independent features added to a flexible item model.
The model relations in Table 1 reinterpret conventional item parameters through the number, arrangement, or spectrum of microstates.
text.formatted: The model relations in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> reinterpret conventional item parameters through the number, arrangement, or spectrum of microstates.

text.text: Local nonmonotonicity arises when the mean slopes of the correct and distractor macrostates reverse their ordering (Theorem 2.1).
The giant-MiRM result (Theorem 3.1) follows by combining item-level microstates across a test.
PRM and the generalized total score then determine the direction and credit of the resulting giant item.
Item characteristics, ICC geometry, test composition, and scoring are therefore different consequences of the same latent-state construction.
In this sense, the microstate representation is mathematically coherent and structurally informative rather than merely a device for adding parameters.
This structural claim should nevertheless be distinguished from a cognitive one.
The response distribution, its local discrimination and difficulty, and a reduced microstate representation are statistical objects.
Calling a particular state a strategy, misconception, reason, or response pathway is an interpretation placed on those objects.

However, this distinction is not peculiar to MiRM: a lower-asymptote parameter can be identified under the 3PL without establishing that the corresponding responses were actually produced by guessing, just as an upper asymptote does not by itself establish slipping.
Likewise, the present results do not show that every fitted microstate corresponds one-to-one with a distinct cognitive process.
Even if such a literal correspondence fails, the geometric, compositional, and information-theoretic results of MiRM remain intact.
Our narrower claim is that microstates provide a common explanatory vocabulary in which previously separate item characteristics can be understood and empirically investigated.
Coarse-graining also places a fundamental limit on that investigation.
The information decomposition in Eq. 212 shows that observing only a macrostate loses information, in the amount of the expected within-macrostate variance of the microstate slopes.
text.formatted: The information decomposition in Eq. <ref type="formula" target="#formula_7">2</ref>12 shows that observing only a macrostate loses information, in the amount of the expected within-macrostate variance of the microstate slopes.

text.text: When several reasons for responding are reduced to the same category, some ability-relevant variation becomes unavailable.
MiRM cannot recover information absent from the observations; it instead uses the structure that remains visible in the aggregate response curves.
Not every microstate, however, must remain entirely latent.
Option choices, response times, eye movements, intermediate work, or verbal reports may anchor particular states and restrict the representations compatible with the data.
Open-ended assessment can be understood similarly as reducing coarse-graining by retaining part of the reasoning that selected-response scoring discards.

With such external anchors, the information lost through coarse-graining may eventually become useful for assessing how clearly an item separates its underlying reasons for correct and incorrect responses.
A stronger cognitive interpretation requires validation against response processes established independently of binary outcomes.

Concept inventories and diagnostic datasets such as the FCI (D. Hestenes et al., 1992), FMCE (Thornton & Sokoloff, 1998), and Eedi (King et al., 2024) offer promising settings because their options are informed by prior accounts of misconceptions or solution processes.

text.text: Microstates estimated from dichotomized responses could be compared with withheld option choices, process measurements, or expert classifications.
Such analyses would directly address whether statistically inferred states predict independently observed response-generating processes.

The information decomposition specifies how much ability-relevant information has been destroyed by dichotomization, although translating that quantity into a bound on the recovery of individual state labels would require additional assumptions.
The behavior of the 3PLQ provides a more indirect illustration of the explanatory value of microstates.
Its quadratic logit corresponds to a Gaussian spectrum of slopes in one macrostate, with the magnitude of the quadratic coefficient representing the variance of that spectrum (see Appendix C.2).
The model can consequently summarize diffuse pathway heterogeneity with a single parameter, helping to explain its strong BIC performance (Table 3).
text.formatted: The model can consequently summarize diffuse pathway heterogeneity with a single parameter, helping to explain its strong BIC performance (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">3</ref>).

text.text: The same account explains its limitation: a Gaussian spectrum is unbounded, whereas a finite MiRM has extremal slopes.
This appears as the extremal reversal of the 3PLQ's ICCs in Figure 7.
text.formatted: This appears as the extremal reversal of the 3PLQ's ICCs in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_8">7</ref>.

text.text: Thus, the central flexibility and problematic tail behavior of the 3PLQ arise from the same structural assumption.

Explaining both the strength and the weakness of a competing model in a common language supports the explanatory usefulness of the microstate representation without requiring every inferred state to be cognitively literal.
When introducing PRM in Section 3.2, we noted that PRM provides several theoretical guarantees for modeling ability, whereas the fit of a flexible model without PRM is unreliable.
Figures 4 and 9 show this clearly; in particular, the upper-left panel of Figure 9 is a typical example of the ICCs that MiRM produces when fitted without PRM.
text.formatted: Figures <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">4</ref> and <ref type="figure" target="#fig_10">9</ref> show this clearly; in particular, the upper-left panel of Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_10">9</ref> is a typical example of the ICCs that MiRM produces when fitted without PRM.

text.text: PRM is therefore essential for fitting MiRM.
Conversely, although PRM was proposed as a property of a test independent of MiRM, it loses its practical meaning in most existing models because they always satisfy PRM.
This shows why MiRM and PRM need to be introduced together.
Moreover, the PRM conditions are available in closed form in MiRM, making their joint use practical.
However, this does not mean that PRM is the single invariant answer for ability measurement.
While PRM has the conceptual strength of scoring invariance, other test-level monotonicity conditions with different properties can also be proposed.
Moving the monotonicity condition from the item to the test has a broader implication.
PRM as a test-level condition implies that item characteristics may change slightly depending on how the test is composed.
Remark 3.2 shows this well: a nonmonotonic item within a test is refitted as monotonic if the item itself is used as a test.
This is not a defect of the condition, but its intended meaning.
What we measure through a test is not the true ability itself.
We only define from the response patterns the tendency that the test, as a measuring device, explains best, and expect that this tendency follows the true ability.
Therefore, whether a test measures the true ability is a question of validity, and it cannot be answered inside the model.
The model only shows the direction on which the items of a test agree.
Whether this direction is the trait that the test was designed for must be checked outside the model.
Without such an investigation, it is difficult to claim that an item's characteristics are strictly intrinsic to the item.
One of the best practical approaches may be to regard the microstates or item characteristics that survive across different test sets and respondent groups as the item's own.
Meanwhile, since an ideal test will automatically generate the best unidimensional explanation, it may pass PRM as a diagnostic criterion even when PRM is not imposed as a constraint.
Furthermore, if the ability path folds back or some ICCs reverse direction when fitted without PRM, as in Figure 9, this may be read as a sign that the test is intrinsically multidimensional.
text.formatted: Furthermore, if the ability path folds back or some ICCs reverse direction when fitted without PRM, as in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_10">9</ref>, this may be read as a sign that the test is intrinsically multidimensional.

text.text: MiRM's unification framework helps not only theory, but also practical item analysis by placing several departures on a single layer.
Before MiRM, practitioners had to choose a specific model in advance to reflect an item's expected behavior-for instance, the 3PL for guessing or the RH model for asymmetry.

However, items within the same test often exhibit different departures, leaving mismatches under any single traditional model, while fitting multiple competing models and comparing their parameters is cumbersome.
In MiRM, the data make this choice instead of the practitioner.
The model captures these departures simultaneously within one model family and summarizes them on a common scale.
Although slight instability in configuration selection and heavier computation remain practical costs, we address these in Section 8.5.
Putting item characteristics on a single layer also changes how we handle nonmonotonicity.
We do not claim that nonmonotonic ICCs are practically healthy, nor do we suggest using nonmonotonic items or negative item credits.
Our claim is narrower: itemwise nonmonotonicity should be detected rather than assumed away, and in rare cases a correct response can indeed serve as negative evidence for ability.
By the results in Section 2.1.2, MiRM can serve as both a diagnostic tool and an operational model in a single step.

If a practitioner prefers all items to be monotonic, MiRM can directly flag nonmonotonic items for revision or removal without a separate misfit analysis, and the stability of 𝜔 𝑗 (𝜃) across ability can guide practical item weights for sum scores.
On the other hand, an educator or researcher who wishes to retain dip items for substantive analysis can use the fitted MiRM directly as the operational scoring model under PRM.
A local dip can also be informative in its own right.

In educational assessment, a dip may capture U-shaped behavioral growth (Strauss, 1991), where intermediate learners temporarily perform worse than novices as they transition from superficial rules to deeper concepts, as suggested by Science 81 in Section 7.3.
text.formatted: In educational assessment, a dip may capture U-shaped behavioral growth <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Strauss, 1991)</ref>, where intermediate learners temporarily perform worse than novices as they transition from superficial rules to deeper concepts, as suggested by Science 81 in Section 7.3.

text.text: Our analysis was restricted to computer-scored items, many of which are selected-response items, where the chance to guess naturally provides a second correct pathway that satisfies Corollary 2.3 (𝑐 ≥ 2).
Detecting a dip in an open-ended or constructed-response item would therefore be an even stronger substantive finding.
Beyond educational testing, nonmonotonic curves over an ordered trait are also natural in psychological measurement.

In Kohlberg's Heinz dilemma (Kohlberg, 1981), for example, the binary decision of whether Heinz should steal the drug can oscillate across stages of moral development even as the underlying reasoning matures monotonically.
text.formatted: In Kohlberg's Heinz dilemma <ref type="bibr">(Kohlberg, 1981)</ref>, for example, the binary decision of whether Heinz should steal the drug can oscillate across stages of moral development even as the underlying reasoning matures monotonically.

text.text: Many psychological items may share this structure when distinct reasons are compressed into a binary choice.
Finally, from the perspective of preventing unintended nonmonotonicity in item writing, Corollary 2.3 offers a counterintuitive lesson.

Traditional item development has focused heavily on crafting plausible distractors, yet a local dip requires at least two correct pathways (𝑐 ≥ 2, such as intended mastery alongside guessing or a shortcut).
To prevent a dip, ensuring that the correct answer is reachable through a single intended pathway (𝑐 = 1) is therefore important, rather than focusing only on distractors.

Conversely, Corollary 2.2 and Section 4 show that diversifying attractive distractors (𝑑 ≥ 2) -long treated as an unquestioned virtue in item design -may enable ICC peaks and flatten discrimination at high ability.

MiRM is primarily a unidimensional parametric IRT model, yet it bridges parametric and nonparametric approaches through the Universal Approximation Theorem (Theorem 4.1). Wei (2026) pursued a similar goal with the Beta-Bernstein IRT model, establishing an expressive space comparable to that of MiRM, though its direct readings into traditional parametric models were limited.

text.text: By contrast, MiRM recovers the structural interpretations of classical models (Section 4) and restores the 2PL parameters locally by microstate statistics (Eq.
Consequently, fitting a MiRM to any nonparametric ICC can serve as an algebraic parameterization filter that equips the curve with interpretable derivatives and state-level readings.

Moreover, because a finite MiRM with sufficiently many states can approximate any continuous ICC on a compact domain, it represents the theoretical ceiling of what a single ordered ability coordinate can explain.

From this perspective, the small gains in performance across models in Table 3 do not mean that MiRM contributes little; rather, they may indicate that the standard 2PL already captures the bulk of the unidimensional signal and that spline and MiRM approach the ceiling, with the per-item MiRM reaching this level parsimoniously.

text.text: In fact, since the 3PLQ and spline are used mainly for fit rather than interpretation, it is fairer to compare MiRM with interpretable models such as the 2PL, 3PL, and RH, where the performance gain is much clearer.

What truly stands outside MiRM are the alternative explanations for unidimensional IRT itself: latent dimensions (Multidimensional IRT; Reckase, 2006), latent populations (Mixture IRT; Mislevy & Verhelst, 1990), group-item relations (DIF; Holland & Wainer, 1993), or item-item relations (Network Psychometrics; Epskamp et al., 2018).

text.text: They account for features that lie outside a single universal, comparable ability 𝜃.
However, just as with the departures within unidimensional IRT models, their representation spaces can still overlap (Kruis & Maris, 2016).

text.text: They can even overlap with the unidimensional departures: Liao et al. (2026) showed that ICC asymmetry can arise when the data are generated from multidimensional latent traits, while MiRM is algebraically related to mixture models (Table 1).

(2026)</ref> showed that ICC asymmetry can arise when the data are generated from multidimensional latent traits, while MiRM is algebraically related to mixture models (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: The fundamental question is therefore which features can be truly reduced to a single ability and which cannot.
Selecting among these external accounts before characterizing the full expressive capacity of an individual item may be conceptually premature.

As we measure people on a single scale rather than teaching or treating them, what the test directly controls is the item, not the person; attributing extra causes of item-person or item-item interactions to each item should therefore precede introducing external traits.
Establishing such a within-item reference family provides a basis against which additional structures can be added.
The RH model (Molenaar, 2015) exemplifies this approach: population-level heteroscedasticity can become an itemwise asymmetry parameter once the pattern arises systematically from the item.
text.formatted: The RH model <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Molenaar, 2015)</ref> exemplifies this approach: population-level heteroscedasticity can become an itemwise asymmetry parameter once the pattern arises systematically from the item.

text.text: In the same sense, MiRM is important because it does as much of this work as possible inside the item.
Although attributing unidimensional explanations to the item as much as possible is a useful starting point, the alternative accounts above are neither meaningless nor absent in real data.

Because MiRM is a flexible model, it can unintentionally absorb local dependence (Bradlow et al., 1999), population-level features, or extra dimensions into its curve, as occasionally seen in MiRM(5, 5).

text.text: In addition, where data are sparse, extreme-tail reversals similar to those of the 3PLQ can occasionally appear, such as in MiRM(5, 5) on Item 16 in Figure 7, while the sharp boundaries in the local characteristics of Item 29 may come from insufficiently dense Gauss-Hermite quadrature nodes.

text.text: Empirically, these issues could be mitigated by bounding the slopes 𝛼 𝑠 , applying PRM to smaller item subsets, using early stopping when the loss plateaus, or increasing the number of quadrature nodes.
However, these remedies are all heuristic, and a more fundamental approach is needed.
Because the algorithm that selects (𝑐, 𝑑) affects all of these issues, improving configuration selection is an important task for future work.

The consistency results in Figure 5, together with the performance and item characteristics in Section 7, show that configurations are selected fairly consistently and that item-specific configurations exist in data.
text.formatted: The consistency results in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">5</ref>, together with the performance and item characteristics in Section 7, show that configurations are selected fairly consistently and that item-specific configurations exist in data.

text.text: One may improve the selection consistency by selecting the most frequent configuration of each item across multiple splits.
Yet we do not claim that our current procedure always finds the optimal configuration for every item.
Specifically, in a preliminary simulation, items generated from (3,1) were recovered poorly and were mostly assigned (2,1).
The algorithm is thus conservative for configurations beyond the (2,2) grid, and the state counts in Figure 5 may be underestimated.
text.formatted: The algorithm is thus conservative for configurations beyond the (2,2) grid, and the state counts in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">5</ref> may be underestimated.

text.text: Part of this limit is fundamental, since ratios of exponential sums are not fully identified (Appendix A.1).
Connecting the theoretical quantities of MiRM to real-world features is equally important.
Although 𝑎(𝜃) and 𝑏(𝜃) are theoretically clear and offer intuitive empirical readings, further validation is needed to establish what cognitive features they actually reflect.
A natural candidate for 𝑎(𝜃) is how deterministically ability governs the response at that level, as seen in the RH derivation (Section 4.3).
If these local characteristics are understood more concretely, they could be directly useful in computerized adaptive testing (CAT) and adaptive learning.
Finally, an important direction for future work lies in the choice of prior.
Fundamentally, MiRM makes no structural assumption on the prior distribution of ability.
As noted earlier, the Gaussian prior 𝜃 ∼ N (0, 1) is a safe and convenient baseline for comparing models, but there is no guarantee that true ability follows a normal distribution on that scale.
In statistical mechanics, choosing the ability scale corresponds to setting the scale of inverse temperature.

Just as temperature has a physical lower bound, setting upper or lower bounds on the ability domain may be substantively meaningful in psychometrics, suggesting that a normal distribution over all real numbers may not always be the most natural choice.

text.text: Our claim is the former, and we examine below whether the dips survive under several alternative explanations.
Several factors can be pointed out as sources of nonmonotonicity, especially data sparsity and group differences.
